p: The poem's first line is also its ancient name, and scholars still argue over what it means.
b: The Akkadian is three words, inūma ilū awīlum, "when gods (were) man." Babylonian scribes named a poem by its first line, and the colophons call this one inūma ilū awīlum (3:65). There are three main readings. W. G. Lambert and A. R. Millard (1969) took awīlum as a comparison: "when the gods were like men." Wolfram von Soden took it as a plain statement: "when the gods were (still) man." The SEAL editors agree with von Soden's grammar but read it as a picture that the next line explains: the gods were "man" because they did a man's work. Michael Streck added that a later copy of the poem replaces the bare wording with an open comparison, kī, "like," which suggests the older line was a metaphor; on that ground the SEAL editors say the translations of Wasserman (2003) and Loesov (2004), which followed Lambert, "should be abandoned." The Plain keeps the bare wording so the reader can feel the puzzle.

t: Gods who work, and a God who does not tire
p: Here the gods are worn out by work. In Genesis God works, then rests, and is never worn out.
b: The poem opens with gods doing hard labor and sinking under it. Genesis also speaks of God working and resting: "on the seventh day he rested from all the work he had been doing" (Genesis 2:2). A. R. Millard noted that the actions are alike but the meaning is opposite: the Babylonian gods were "like a man," toiling and tiring, while the God of Genesis "needed not to labour for His sustenance, nor did He tire of His work." Isaiah says the same: "He never tires, and he never wears out" (Isaiah 40:28). Differs: the Bible's God rests because his work is finished, not because he is exhausted.

p: Tupšikku is the frame or basket for carrying earth and bricks, the badge of forced labor.
b: The tupšikku was the basket or frame that laborers carried on their heads or backs, full of earth or bricks. The SEAL editors note that it stands for the work itself. It is the poem's symbol of drudgery: the gods carry it now, and humans will carry it after 3:10. Israel remembered the same burden from Egypt, where the LORD says of his people, "his palms let go of the basket" (Psalm 81:6). The Hebrew word there, dud, is a different word for the same kind of load.

p: The number seven could belong to the Anunnaki or to the Igigi. Scholars split.
b: The Akkadian sebettam, "seven, a group of seven," stands at the end of line 5, where the Anunnaki are named. Lambert and Millard (1969), Lambert again in 1980, and Benjamin Foster joined it to the Anunnaki; A. R. Millard's 1967 lecture renders the line "The great Anunnaku, the Seven." Von Soden and the SEAL editors join it to the Igigi in the next line, because of the grammar of the word: the great Anunnaki made the seven Igigi do the work. The Plain follows SEAL. Either way the picture is clear: senior gods, junior gods, and a heavy load passed downward.

p: Two ranks of gods: the Anunnaki in charge, the Igigi doing the labor.
b: In this poem the Anunnaki are the great gods who rule, and the Igigi are the junior gods who dig and carry. A. R. Millard summed up the opening as "the junior gods (the Igigu) labouring at the behest of the senior deities (the Anunnaku)." The site spells them the way English readers usually meet them: Anunnaki and Igigi.

p: Anu, Enlil, Ninurta and Ennugi: a heavenly court, with titles taken from a Babylonian palace.
b: The list reads like a royal court. Anu, the sky god, is father and king. Enlil is the "counselor," the one who actually governs the earth (the SEAL editors suggest a play on malku, "ruler"). Ninurta, Enlil's warrior son, is the guzalû, "throne-bearer," a palace official. Ennugi is the gallû, an officer who enforces orders; the same word later names a kind of demon. Lambert and Millard argued for this reading over gugallu, "canal inspector," and the late Sippar copy published in 1996 confirmed it. The gods' world copies the human state, with its kings, officials and labor gangs.

p: The gods seem to hold hands as part of a ritual of casting lots.
b: Older editions read the first word differently: von Soden read "box (of lots)." Andrew George and Farouk al-Rawi checked the tablet and read the sign as "hand." The SEAL editors take it as the gods holding hands while they cast the lot, as Lambert and Millard had already suggested. The late Sippar copy confirmed the word for "side." The scene is a solemn sharing-out, not a quarrel.

p: Three gods draw lots for sky, earth and the waters. In the Bible the whole world already belongs to the LORD.
b: Anu takes heaven, Enlil the earth, Enki the waters below. Homer's Iliad has a close picture: Poseidon says that when the lots were shaken he won the sea, Hades the darkness and Zeus the broad heaven (Iliad 15.187-193). The Bible also knows a division, but God makes it and owns everything: "To the LORD belong the earth and all that fills it" (Psalm 24:1); "The heavens are the LORD's own heavens, / and the earth is his gift to human beings" (Psalm 115:16). Even a lot is in his hand: "every verdict it gives comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). Differs: no realm is left to another god.

p: Enlil gets the earth "as his subjects." Psalm 115 says God gave the earth to human beings.
b: In the poem the earth is Enlil's domain, and its people are his subjects; humans will be made to serve there. Psalm 115:16 turns this around: "The heavens are the LORD's own heavens, / and the earth is his gift to human beings." Genesis gives humans rule over the earth under God (Genesis 1:28). Deuteronomy 32:8-9 pictures the Most High dividing the nations while keeping Jacob as his own share. That passage is the closest biblical match to a sharing-out among heavenly powers, and readers differ on it (see the topic page).

a: The bolt and rope that lock in the sea
p: The sea is held back by a bolt and given to Enki to guard. Job and the Psalms use the same picture for God.
b: The SEAL editors explain the two nouns, "bolt" and "snare-rope," as one locking device: a bar tied fast with rope, which keeps the salt sea from flooding the land and the fresh water. A. R. Millard saw here no battle with the sea, only a sea that needs to be kept in its place, and compared Genesis 1:9 and the passages where God sets limits for the sea. Job 38:10 uses the same image: "when I carved out my boundary for it / and put up a bolt and doors." Agrees in the picture; differs in who holds the bolt.

p: Enki is his Sumerian name, Ea his Akkadian one. The site uses Enki throughout.
b: The Old Babylonian copy calls this god Enki and gives him the title naššiku; the late Sippar copy here says Ea and spells the title niššīku. SEAL's glossary explains the word as "a title of Ea, prince." Enki and Ea are the same god: lord of the fresh waters under the earth, wise, skilled in spells and crafts, and the friend of humans in this poem. The site keeps "Enki" in every verse, as the brief for this book directs, and notes where a copy says Ea. He will plan the making of humans (3:26) and later warn Atrahasis of the Flood.

p: The fresh waters under the earth, Enki's home.
b: Apsû is the deep body of fresh water that Mesopotamians believed lay under the earth, feeding springs and rivers. It is Enki's realm (see 2:66, "king of the Apsu"). The Bible speaks of "the springs of the great deep" that burst open at the Flood (Genesis 7:11), but there the deep is part of what God made, not the home of a god.

a: The gods were digging the rivers
p: In a land with little rain, life depended on canals. Digging them was the hardest forced labor.
b: Southern Iraq gets little rain, so farming depended on water led from the Tigris and Euphrates through canals. Kings called up their subjects every year to dig and clean them. Millard notes that this canal work was the labor later thought fit for the lowest rank. The SEAL editors point out that an Assyrian king's inscriptions also call canals "the life of the land." The poem imagines the gods themselves doing this work before humans existed.

p: The same two rivers flow out of Eden in Genesis. Here the gods dig them.
b: Genesis names four rivers that flow from Eden, among them "The third river is named Tigris. It flows east of Assyria. The fourth river is the Euphrates" (Genesis 2:14). Millard observed that Genesis names the rivers and traces their courses but tells nothing of their making, while here the gods dig them by hand. Differs: in Genesis the river "goes out from Eden to water the garden" (Genesis 2:10) as a gift; here the rivers are the fruit of the gods' sweat.

p: The Akkadian says only "that of the basket"; the SEAL editors take it to mean reeds.
b: The words ša tupšikki mean "that of the basket." Baskets were woven from reeds, and the next line mentions a great reed marsh, so the SEAL editors explain the phrase as the reeds. The lines around it are badly broken, but they seem to say that the gods made the marshes along with the rivers and mountains. The Plain keeps the Akkadian's wording and adds the editors' explanation in brackets.

p: The numbers are broken. Most likely they climb by tens: ten, twenty, thirty, forty years.
b: These three lines survive only in the Assyrian copy from Nineveh, and the number at the start of each is broken. The SEAL editors restore 10, 20 and 30 years, with a question mark, which would lead up to the "forty years" of 1:41; so the Plain shows the gaps. Von Soden once read a far larger figure in 1:41 (2,500 years), but the SEAL editors, with Lambert and Millard, read forty.

a: The gods bore the work by night and by day
p: The gods' work never stops. The Bible sets a limit on work for every worker, slave and animal.
b: The gods labor "by night and by day," with no day off. The Law of Moses gave Israel's workers a weekly rest, and Jesus said, "The Sabbath came into being for the sake of human beings, and not human beings for the sake of the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27). Humans in this poem will be made to take over an endless load; in the Bible, God himself commands rest for those who labor. Answers back: the Bible's Creator gives rest instead of taking it.

p: The Akkadian idiom is "to eat someone's pieces," meaning to accuse them. Daniel uses the same idiom in Aramaic.
b: The words are ikkalū karṣī, literally "they were eating pieces." The SEAL editors explain karṣī akālu as "to accuse somebody in front of a third party"; the Plain renders it "accuse" here and in Enki's question at 3:3, where the same idiom comes back. The same idiom appears in the Aramaic of Daniel: the Chaldeans "ate the pieces of the Jews" (Daniel 3:8, Aramaic akhalu qartsehon), which the site's Plain renders "slandered the Jews"; again in Daniel 6:24. The junior gods are grumbling against the gods above them.

a: This work basket is killing us!
t: Lines from a Middle Babylonian copy
p: These two lines survive only in a copy from Babylon now in Montserrat, Spain.
b: Verses 2:3-2:4 (lines 40a-40b) are found only in a Middle Babylonian tablet from Babylon, now in the Museu Bíblic de Montserrat (MM 818), published by Barbara Böck and Ignacio Márquez Rowe. It is several centuries younger than the main Old Babylonian copy and sometimes adds or changes lines. The cry "the basket is killing us" comes back in the rebels' answer (2:125).

a: come, let us lift him out of his seat!
t: "Let us lift him from his seat"
p: A call to remove Enlil from power: the strikers want to unseat their boss.
b: The verb našû means "to lift, carry," and šubtu is "seat, dwelling." To lift a ruler from his seat is to depose him. Millard summed up the scene: the gods "decided to depose their taskmaster, Enlil." The rebels sing the line four times (2:8, 2:10, 2:22, 2:24), like a chant.
orig: i ni-iš-ši-a i-na šu-ub-ti-šu (i niššiā ina šubtišu)

t: We: the god who leads the strike?
p: The god who rouses the strikers is named We, the same name as the god who is later slain to make humans.
b: The name is We, a god's name, not the English word "we." The old copy keeps its last sign, and the late Sippar copy writes it with the sign NAGAR, which the SEAL editors read as We, following Manfred Krebernik, and not as Alla, as it was once read. The Middle Babylonian copy adds "who has understanding" (see the variant), the words used of the god slain in 3:48. If the readings are right, the god who stirs up the rebellion is the god who dies for it. Some modern writers join the name with the next word, as Tikva Frymer-Kensky does with "We-ilu, a god who has sense," from 3:48, where the old copy follows the name with ila, "god"; this line has only We, so the Plain does too. On 3:48 the SEAL editors' English still gives the late copies' name as "Alla," though their comment on this line reads the sign as We; the Plain follows the comment.
orig: A: [{d}we]-⌈e⌉ (We); ba: {d}e10(NAGAR); MM-MB: <{d}>e ša i-šu-ú i-lu ṭe-ma

p: "He opened his mouth to speak, and said to...": the standard way an Akkadian poem starts a speech.
b: The two-line formula pâšu īpušamma izakkar ana introduces almost every speech in the poem, and this site renders it the same way every time. Hebrew and Greek narrative have a similar phrase: "Job opened his mouth and cursed his day" (Job 3:1); "Then he opened his mouth to teach them" (Matthew 5:2). Such formulas helped a singer or reader mark who was speaking.
orig: pí-a-šu i-pu-ša-am-ma / i-za-kàr a-na (pâšu īpušamma izakkar ana)

t: "Before us," or "they did not offer incense"
p: The old copy keeps a trace. The Middle Babylonian copy reads "... before us"; two Assyrian copies seem to say "they did not offer incense."
b: The old copy keeps only a trace here, so the Plain follows the Middle Babylonian copy, which ends the line "... before us." Two Assyrian copies from Nineveh have something like "... they did not offer incense," though the SEAL editors mark those signs as uncertain (see the variant). If the Assyrian reading belongs here, the strikers are also refusing to honor the gods above them with offerings, which would make the strike a religious revolt as well as a labor one.

p: The rebels seem to call Enlil, or his enforcer, "the evil god."
b: Only ilam lemnam, "the evil (or hostile) god," survives in the line. From the context it most likely refers to Enlil, or to the officer who drives them. The rebels do not doubt that Enlil is a god; they think he is a bad master.

a: Enlil has dragged out our yoke
p: The rebels call their work a yoke. The LORD tells Israel he broke the bars of their yoke.
b: Nīru is the wooden beam laid on the necks of oxen. The rebels say Enlil has kept it on them too long. The LORD reminds Israel: "I broke the bars of your yoke and made you walk upright" (Leviticus 26:13). The gods' complaint is the cry of every forced laborer; in the Bible, the God of Israel is the one who hears it (Exodus 3:7).

p: Three Akkadian words for battle are packed into two lines.
b: Tuqumtu, taḫāzu and qablu all mean battle. The second line literally says "let us mix combat and battle," which the SEAL editors call a zeugma, one verb yoked to two nouns. The heaping-up shows the rebels working themselves up to fight.
orig: ti-si-a tu-qú-um-tam / ta-ḫa-za i ni-ib-lu-la qá-ab-la-am

a: They threw fire on their tools
p: The strikers burn their spades and baskets, the things that tied them to the work.
b: The gods set fire to their tools, spades and baskets. Reed baskets and wooden handles burn easily, and burning them says the work is over. Millard retold it: "they set fire to their tools and advanced to force Enlil to relieve them."

p: The Akkadian names the fire itself as a god, Girra.
b: The line says the strikers gave their baskets to Girra (written BIL.GI), the god of fire. In Babylonian thought fire was a god who could be called on in spells. In the Bible fire is God's servant: "He makes the winds into his messengers / and a blazing fire into his servants" (Psalm 104:4).

p: The night was split into watches. The rebels come at its darkest point.
b: Mišil maṣṣarti, "half of the watch," places the attack in the middle of the night. Israel also divided the night into watches: Gideon attacked "at the start of the middle watch" (Judges 7:19). A night raid on a sleeping master is the plan of rebels who expect no mercy.

p: "Mountain House": Enlil's great temple at Nippur.
b: The Ekur (Sumerian "Mountain House") was Enlil's temple at Nippur. The poem pictures the gods' rebellion as a crowd surrounding a real temple, the house a Babylonian hearer knew as the seat of Enlil's rule over the earth.

a: They heard the noise of the Igigi
t: The first noise is the gods' noise
p: Claude's theory: the noise that later angers Enlil may begin here, with the gods. The poem's later lines point another way too.
b: Rigmu, "noise," is a key word of the poem: later Enlil sends plague, drought and flood because human noise keeps him awake. But the first noise in the story is made by the striking gods at his door, and when humans are made Mami says, "You have given noise to humankind" (3:76). My reading: the poem may be hinting that human noise is the old cry of overworked laborers, handed down from the gods. Against this: when the noise comes back, the poem ties it to the land growing wide and the people growing many (Atrahasis 5:2), and Tikva Frymer-Kensky, following Anne Kilmer and William Moran, reads the gods' problem as overpopulation; she does not draw the link to the gods' strike, and the link is my own. In the Bible the cry of the oppressed is heard by God, not hated by him (Exodus 2:23; Exodus 3:7).

a: he got him up out of his bed
p: Enlil has to be woken. Israel's God "does not doze and does not sleep."
b: The ruler of the earth is asleep while his house is besieged, and his servant must wake him. Elijah mocked Baal in the same way: "maybe he's asleep, and he'll wake up" (1 Kings 18:27). Israel sang of its God, "the one who guards Israel / does not doze and does not sleep" (Psalm 121:4). Enlil's need for sleep comes back as the reason for the Flood: human noise keeps him awake. Differs at the root: the Bible's God needs no rest to recover.

p: The word for weapons is partly restored and not certain.
b: Von Soden's reading kakkī, "weapons," fits the traces, but the SEAL editors note that the spelling is unusual and the verb rare with this object, so some doubt remains. The picture is of a frightened ruler arming his house.

p: Nusku is Enlil's sukkallu, his minister or chief servant.
b: A sukkallu in a Babylonian court was the chief minister who carried messages and spoke for the king. Nusku plays that part for Enlil: he is woken first, guards the door, calms his master and goes out to question the rebels. Kalkal, who woke him, is the servant at the door who checks the bolt (2:39).

a: your face has gone pale as tamarisk
p: Enlil's face turns grey-white with fear, like the pale wood of the tamarisk.
b: The Akkadian is a four-word sound play, bēlī bīnu bunūka, "my lord, tamarisk (is) your face." Von Soden and the SEAL editors explain the tamarisk as a picture of a face gone pale. Enlil's answer is lost, but Nusku's words show the great god of the earth shaking before the junior gods.

p: The great gods meet as a court. The Bible also pictures a heavenly council, but God alone rules it.
b: Enlil calls Anu and Enki and the great Anunnaki; a hearing (dīnu) begins, and the gods will decide by vote (3:43). The Bible also shows a heavenly court: Micaiah saw "the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing beside him" (1 Kings 22:19); "God takes his stand in the assembly of El" (Psalm 82:1). Differs: in the Bible the members of the council are God's creatures and servants, and God judges them (Psalm 82:6-7); here the gods are equals who argue, vote and fear one another.

a: Gods, what is this I am seeing?
p: One word is read two ways: as "O gods!" or as "my eye."
b: Lambert and Millard (1969) read i-ni, "my eye": "what has my eye seen?" Von Soden read i-lí, a call to the gods, and the late Sippar copy, which seems to have "gods" here, supports him. The SEAL editors follow von Soden and hear Enlil's shock in the sentence: "O gods, what have I, I myself, seen?"

t: Lines found only in an Assyrian copy
p: Lines 2:75-2:80 are known only from the Assyrian copy, and they already mention the birth goddess.
b: This stretch (lines 110a-110g) survives only in the Assyrian copy from Nineveh; the SEAL editors note that no other copy has these lines, and the old copy runs straight from 2:74 to 2:81 (see the variant). It names Belet-ili, "Lady of the gods," the birth goddess also called Mami and Nintu (see 3:8), and someone says "Call out one god," the words Enlil uses in the Assyrian copy at 2:151.

p: Zikru, usually "word, name," here means "the reason for."
b: Anu asks for the reason behind the siege. The SEAL editors, after George and al-Rawi, note this less common sense of zikru. Anu, unlike Enlil, wants to know why the rebels have come before deciding what to do.

a: Who is the god who leads this battle?
p: Enlil wants a ringleader. The rebels answer that all of them are responsible.
b: The question is asked three times: who is the bēl qablim, the "lord of the battle"? The rebels refuse to name anyone: "All of us together have called for war" (2:122). Yet the council ends by choosing one god to die (2:151; 3:33). If the We who called the gods to revolt at 2:11 is the We slain at 3:48, the one who started the strike is the one who dies. The poem itself does not say why this god is chosen beyond his "understanding" (3:48).

p: A note on the edge of a late Sippar copy: the scribe wrote it down as someone read it out.
b: On the upper edge of one of the late copies from Sippar, published by George and al-Rawi, the scribe wrote what is read as ana pî šaṭir, "written according to the mouth," that is, from dictation; the SEAL editors mark two of its signs as uncertain. If the reading is right, it is a small window into how the poem was copied: one person reading aloud, probably a teacher or senior scribe, and another writing.

t: Gods who rebel: the Igigi and the Bible's fallen angels
p: A revolt of gods. The Bible and 1 Enoch also tell of heavenly rebels, for very different reasons.
b: The Igigi revolt because the work is too hard, and the poem takes their side: Enki agrees they have been wronged (3:3-3:4). In the Bible, rebellion in heaven is sin. Isaiah's "Shining One" says, "I will make myself the Most High's equal" (Isaiah 14:14); Revelation tells of a "war in heaven" in which the dragon and "his angels were thrown down with him" (Revelation 12:7-9); Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 speak of angels who left their place. Helge Kvanvig (2011, as quoted at intertextual.bible) compared the Mesopotamian and Enochic stories: in Atrahasis the lower gods' rebellion led to the making of humans to toil, while in the Watchers story of 1 Enoch the rebellion led to giants for whom humans had to toil. Differs: the Bible's rebels are proud, not overworked, and God is not afraid of them.

a: The work basket has been killing us
p: The gods cry out under forced labor, as Israel did in Egypt. The answers are opposite.
b: Israel in Egypt knew the same work: "hard labor in clay and bricks" (Exodus 1:14). "The Israelites sighed from their labor and cried out" (Exodus 2:23), and the LORD said, "I have heard their outcry because of the men who drive them" (Exodus 3:7). He freed them. In the poem the gods' outcry is answered by making new slaves to take their place. Answers back: the God of the Bible frees laborers; the gods of the poem pass the load down to humans.

a: has agreed to fight it out with Enlil
p: An idiom for a decision taken by all: "our mouth brought (us) to fight with Enlil."
b: The Akkadian ubla pīni mitḫuṣa itti Enlil says literally "our mouth has brought fighting with Enlil." It means the whole group spoke as one and decided. In 2:141 the old copy has a different word in place of "fight" that no one has yet read with confidence; the SEAL editors leave it open.

a: My lord, to the place you sent me
p: Nusku repeats the rebels' words almost exactly. Ancient storytellers liked messages told twice.
b: The poem repeats the message three times: as Enlil gives it (2:95-2:102), as Nusku delivers it (2:108-2:115), and as he reports the answer (2:131-2:141). Akkadian, Ugaritic and Hebrew stories often do this. Genesis 24 has Abraham's servant retell his whole errand to Laban, after saying, "I will not eat until I have told my errand" (Genesis 24:33). Hearers enjoyed the repetition and noticed every small change.

t: A god who weeps for himself
p: Enlil weeps from fear. In the Bible, God grieves over others, and Jesus weeps beside a grave.
b: Enlil, the strongest god of the earth, weeps when he hears that all the Igigi are against him, and dreads what he now knows. The Bible also speaks of God's grief: "it pained him to his heart" (Genesis 6:6), and at Lazarus' tomb, "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). Differs: Enlil's tears are for his own danger; the Bible's God grieves over the ruin of his creatures.

a: I will go up with you to heaven
t: "I will go up" or "my noble one"?
p: Enlil either threatens to leave the earth for heaven, or addresses Anu as "my noble one."
b: The Akkadian e-te-el-li can be read two ways. Lambert and Millard (1969), George and al-Rawi, and Foster read etellī, "my noble one," a title for Anu. Pettinato, von Soden, Shehata and the SEAL editors read etellī, "I will go up," from the verb elû: Enlil threatens to leave the earth and go up to heaven with Anu. The Plain follows the second reading, which makes Enlil ready to give up his rule.

t: The decree: one word in 2:149 and 2:151
p: Parṣu, "decree, office," appears in this line and again in 2:151. Is Enlil giving up his rule, or handing Anu the judgment?
b: Parṣam tabal-mi liqe qāt idika: "carry off the parṣu, take the hand of your strength." SEAL glosses parṣu "office; (cultic) ordinance," a god's assigned rule or decree. The same word comes back two lines later, where the council is to "lay the parṣu" on one god (2:151), so the Plain uses "decree" in both places. Read with "I will go up with you to heaven" (2:148), Enlil may be handing his rule to Anu. The SEAL editors' own English, "Carry the regulation, bring your force!", points instead to Anu taking up the decision; their comment on 2:151 says that to throw the parṣu on someone means "to make him bear the decision," so that the chosen god will be slaughtered. The line is broken in the late copy and not found in the old one, so the question stays open.
orig: bb: [pa]-ar-ṣa-a[m ta-ba-a]l-mi l[i-qé q]a-at ⌈i⌉-[di-ka]; K(+)M-NA: par-ṣa-am ta-ba-a[l-mi ...]

p: Claude's theory: the poem's "one god" who bears the sentence for the many is a dark mirror of the gospel.
b: The SEAL editors read the line as laying the decree on one god, "to make him bear the decision," so that he will be slaughtered (3:33). The high priest Caiaphas said of Jesus, "it is to your advantage that one man should die on behalf of the people" (John 11:50). My reading: the poem and the Gospel share the shape "one dies for the many," but the meaning is reversed. Here a god dies so that other gods may rest and humans may be made into laborers; in the Gospel the Son of Man "came to serve, and to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (Matthew 20:28), to set people free. This is a likeness of shape, not a source: there is no sign that the New Testament writers knew this poem.

p: Enki does not blame the strikers. He says their work really is too heavy and proposes a new worker.
b: In the Old Babylonian copy, Enki speaks for the rebels: "Their work is heavy, their hardship is great." The SEAL editors note that in this old version Enki steps in and starts the making of humans, while in the later copies Anu simply answers (see the variant). Enki's sympathy is real but limited: his answer to the gods' suffering is to make someone else suffer in their place. He is the same god who will later save Atrahasis from the Flood. Enki's question uses the same idiom as 2:1, "eating pieces," to accuse.

p: The end of the line is broken. The SEAL editors wonder whether the earth is pictured as bleeding.
b: The late Sippar copy and an Assyrian copy have a verb that the SEAL editors can only match with nâṭu, a word for a urinary or bowel illness, and they ask whether the line pictures the earth bleeding. The Plain leaves the gap.

p: Tukku is "oppression." The late copy adds: "we hear the noise."
b: The old copy says tukkum kabit, "the oppression is heavy." The late Sippar copy has "the work is heavy, and we hear the noise." Either way, Enki names the gods' labor as harsh treatment, and the late copy ties it to the noise (rigmu) that runs through the whole poem (see 2:41).

p: One goddess with three names: Mami, Nintu ("Lady of birth") and Belet-ili ("Lady of the gods").
b: The mother goddess is called Mami (or Mama) in some lines, Nintu in others (3:23, 3:36), and Belet-ili in others (3:93). The poem explains the last name: after she makes humans the gods call her "Mistress of All the Gods" (3:83). She is a šassūru, a word for the womb and for a birth goddess; the SEAL editors note that the scribe spells it with the sign for "heart," and that her emblem was a sign shaped like a womb. The site keeps whichever name each line uses.

a: Let the birth goddess make a human being
t: "Let us make humankind": two councils, two purposes
p: Both stories have a divine council decide to make humans. They differ on why.
b: The gods' council resolves to make a lullû, a first human, "and let man carry the god's work basket." Genesis also opens with a decision: "Let us make humankind in our image, as our likeness. Let them rule..." (Genesis 1:26). Gerhard Hasel argued that Genesis 1 deliberately contradicts the Mesopotamian picture of humans made "to provide the gods with food": in Genesis God blesses humankind, gives them rule over the earth and gives them food (Genesis 1:28-29); they serve no hungry gods. Answers back: humans are made to rule as God's image, not to replace tired gods.

p: Lullû means a human being in a raw, first state, the first of its kind.
b: SEAL glosses lullû "primeval man." The late Sippar copy writes it with Sumerian signs (LÚ.U18.LU) and adds amēlu, "man," as if to explain it. It is a word for a human made to a plan, before the long line of human births begins. The Plain uses "human being" for lullû and "man" for awīlum, so the gloss at 3:9 gives the Akkadian word.

a: let man carry the god's work basket
t: Made to carry the basket, or to tend the garden?
p: The poem's humans are made to carry the gods' load. Genesis' first human is set in a garden to work and guard it.
b: Millard saw that Genesis "has something in common with this": "The LORD God took the man and settled him in the garden of Eden to work it and to guard it" (Genesis 2:15). But in Genesis the garden already grows, and the hard toil comes only after the man's sin: "By the sweat of your face you will eat bread" (Genesis 3:19). Work in Eden is a calling, not a punishment, and it serves God's world rather than feeding hungry gods. Agrees that humans are made to work; differs on why, and on whose fault the toil is.

p: Abšānu is the yoke or harness of a draft animal.
b: The gods speak of the human as a beast of burden: "let him bear the yoke." The word abšānu is the harness or yoke on an ox. In 3:21 it is called "the work of Enlil." Compare the yoke the rebels complained of in 2:19.

t: Mami and Eve, "mother of everyone living"
p: Who's who: is the mother goddess an echo of Eve? The likeness is a title, not a person. Verdict: unlikely.
b: Mami is "maker of humankind" (bāniat awīlūti), and Genesis says Eve was "the mother of everyone living" (Genesis 3:20). What fits: both are named as the source of human life. What does not: Mami is a goddess who shapes humans from clay and blood and helps at births; Eve is a human woman, made by God and named by Adam, who gives birth as every mother does. Nothing in the two stories joins them beyond the title. No study opened for this page argues that they are the same figure. Verdict: unlikely to be the same figure; the likeness shows only that both peoples asked where life begins.

a: Let him bear the yoke, the work of Enlil.
t: A heavy yoke, and a light one
p: Humans are made to wear Enlil's yoke. Jesus offers his own yoke, and rest with it.
b: The gods' plan is that humans will bear "the work of Enlil" for ever. Jesus said to the worn out: "Lift my yoke onto yourselves and learn from me ... And you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is kind to wear, and the load I give is light" (Matthew 11:29-30). Answers back: in the poem the yoke passes from tired gods to humans; in the Gospel the Son of God calls the loaded-down to himself and gives rest. There is no sign that Jesus had this poem in mind; the contrast is the reader's.

p: Enki is the god of skill, magic and the fresh waters, and the clay comes from his realm.
b: Nintu says she cannot make humans alone. Enki is the god of the Apsu, the fresh water under the earth, and of purifying rites and spells, and he is "the one who makes everything clean." Millard noted that the clay "was provided by Enki, presumably from the Apsu, his realm." Making a human takes the waters and wisdom of Enki and the womb-skill of the mother goddess together.

a: Let him hand me the clay
p: Here two gods share the work of shaping man from clay. In the Bible God himself is the potter.
b: The picture of a maker shaping people from clay is shared: "the LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground" (Genesis 2:7); "We are the clay, and you are the one who shaped us" (Isaiah 64:8); "as clay is in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand" (Jeremiah 18:6); "you shaped me as from clay" (Job 10:9). Millard argued that the earthy side of human nature is something people could conclude from nature anywhere, and need not come from a common source. Differs: in the Bible the one God plans, shapes and gives life; here one god supplies the clay, another shapes it, and the council votes.

a: the seventh and the fifteenth day of the month
t: The first, seventh and fifteenth days
p: Days of the moon's month set aside for rites. The fifteenth, šapattu, is the full moon, not a Sabbath.
b: Arḫu is the first day of the month (new moon), sebūtu the seventh, šapattu the fifteenth. The SEAL editors connect the rite with the monthly moon festivals, at which the king was purified by bathing. The word šapattu sounds like Hebrew shabbat, and, as Millard noted, emphasis "is often laid" on the likeness. Millard answered that the Akkadian word "denotes specifically the full moon ... on the fifteenth day of the lunar month, and nothing else," and that "no derived Sabbath existed in Babylonia." Israel's Sabbath counts sevens of days from creation (Genesis 2:2-3), not phases of the moon.

a: Let them butcher a single god
p: The verb is the butcher's word for slaughtering an animal. The Bible never tells of God making man from a dead god.
b: Ṭabāḫu is to slaughter, as one slaughters a sheep. Millard noted that the slaughter of a god to make humans is found in other Babylonian myths too (Enuma Elish tablet VI), but "no hint of the use of dead deity or any material part of a living one is found in Genesis." In the Bible, life is God's gift breathed into dust (Genesis 2:7), and death comes in with sin (Genesis 3:19), not before the first human exists.

a: let the gods be made clean in it
t: Cleansed by it, or from it?
p: The gods are cleansed in connection with the slaughter, but how is unclear.
b: The words litellilū ilū ina qerbi, "let the gods be pure in the midst of it," come from the second Old Babylonian copy (E) and a late Sippar copy, since the main copy is broken here. George and al-Rawi read them as the gods being purified "thereby." The SEAL editors object that blood is the chief thing that makes unclean, so bathing in it could hardly purify; they suggest "from it," with a question mark, that is, the gods cleanse themselves from the killing. The Plain keeps the open "in it." The editors also cite Eckart Frahm's remark on the link between destroying a guilty god, purifying the others, and creating man. The Bible links blood and cleansing in the opposite way: "almost everything is made clean with blood" (Hebrews 9:22).

a: Out of his flesh and his blood
p: Humans are made from a god's flesh and blood. The Bible also says life is in the blood, but it belongs to God.
b: In the poem, a god's flesh and blood are mixed into the clay, so something of a god lives in every human. The Bible also ties life to blood: "For a body's life is in its blood" (Leviticus 17:11), and so human blood may not be shed, "for in God's image / he made humankind" (Genesis 9:6). Agrees that blood is life and that something of the divine marks humans. Differs: in the Bible that mark is God's image, not a slain god's body, and blood is given back to God on the altar, not used as raw material.

p: In Akkadian, awīlum "man" sounds as if it holds both We, the slain god's name, and ilum, "god."
b: The SEAL editors, following Manfred Krebernik, note that the slain god's name We plays on awīlum, "man" (and on the cry "woe"), and that one late Sippar copy spells "and man" as u wa-wilum, which recalls the name. The poem seems to say with sounds what it says with the clay: the human is made of a god, ilu, and of the god We. Compare the first line of the poem (1:1).
orig: i-lu-um-ma ù a-wi-lum (ilumma u awīlum); bb: i-lum-ma u wa-wi-lum

p: The gods want to hear a drum for all time. Claude's suggestion: the beating of the human heart.
b: The word is uppu, a drum. The SEAL editors note that the late Sippar copy misread it as a verb, "let him appear," and that later temple texts reused these lines. The poem does not say what the drum is. My suggestion: since it comes from the god's flesh along with the ghost, it may be the beat of the heart or pulse that marks a living body. The Bible speaks of God knitting the body in the womb (Psalm 139:13) and of the spirit going back to God at death (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

a: Let a ghost come out of the god's flesh
p: A wordplay: the slain god had ṭēmu, "understanding," and from his flesh comes the eṭemmu, "ghost."
b: The god chosen to die is the one "who had understanding" (ṭēmu, 3:48). From his flesh comes the eṭemmu, the ghost or spirit that survives a person's death. The SEAL editors note that the old copy spells it we-ṭi-im-mu, which recalls both We and ṭēmu, and they call the eṭemmu "the essential trait of man." So humans carry a dead god's understanding and a ghost that will outlast them.

a: Let it make the living know its sign
p: The ghost is to be a sign to the living, but the grammar allows several readings.
b: The words balṭa ittašu lišēdīšu are short and hard. The SEAL editors understand them as the ghost making itself known to the living as the man's own sign. Others have read them differently, as Shehata and Foster record. What is clear is the next line: the ghost exists "so that he will never be forgotten."

t: A ghost, or a living soul?
p: The poem gives humans a ghost to keep their memory. Genesis gives a breath of life from God himself.
b: In Atrahasis the divine part of a human is a dead god's flesh and the ghost that comes from it, a shade that will go to the underworld. In Genesis God "blew into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being" (Genesis 2:7), and at death "the spirit goes back to God, who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7). Agrees that humans have a part that outlasts the body; differs on where it comes from and where it goes.

p: Pāqidū šīmāti: the great gods who assign each thing its lot.
b: Šīmtu is a fixed destiny, the lot given to a person or thing. The Anunnaki are those who "care for" or oversee the fates. The whole council agrees to the plan, so the making of humans is a decision of all the great gods.

t: The name of the slain god: We, We-ila, Alla
p: The old copy writes "We, a god"; the late copies use a sign once read "Alla." The Plain says "We, the god," as the old line runs.
b: The old copy writes dWe-e i-la ša išû ṭēma, "We, a god who had understanding," and the Plain follows that order: "We, the god who had understanding." Some writers join the first two words into one name (Frymer-Kensky: "We-ilu"); the site gives the name as We, as the line at 2:11 has it, and renders ila once, as "the god." The late Sippar copies use the sign NAGAR, once read Alla; the SEAL editors, following Manfred Krebernik, read it as We in their comment on 2:11, though their English for this line still prints "Alla." They also note that the late copy puts ilam, "god," in the wrong place, and that the word order of the related line in the Middle Babylonian copy (2:11) probably comes from a scribe confusing išû and ilu. In the late copies Enlil is named as behind the killing (see 3:49 and the variants). On the wordplay with awīlum, "man," see 3:37; on his "understanding" (ṭēmu), see 3:40.
orig: A: {d}we-e i-la ša i-šu-ú ṭe4-e-ma; bb: {d}alla(NAGAR) ša i-šu-ú i-lam ṭè-e-ma

t: Who's who: We, Adam, and the blood of Christ
p: Is the slain god a memory of anyone in the Bible? Verdict: unlikely. The contrast is still worth seeing.
b: Is We, the god whose death gives humans life and understanding, an echo of the first man or of the Bible's teaching on blood? What fits: his blood is mixed into the first humans, and Genesis says human blood carries God's image (Genesis 9:6). What does not: he is a god put to death against his will to free other gods from work; Adam is a man made from dust; and nothing in Genesis is made from a dead body. Verdict: unlikely to be a memory of any biblical figure. On the deeper contrast with Christ's blood, see the note at 3:50.

p: The council killed him. A late copy adds that Enlil was behind it.
b: The old copy simply says they slaughtered him "in their assembly." The late Sippar copy adds Enlil's name in the line; the SEAL editors take it to mean that Enlil did not kill the god himself but was behind the decision. The death is a public act of the whole council.

a: Out of his flesh and his blood
t: A god's blood, and "his own blood"
p: Claude's theory: the poem and the New Testament both tie life to divine blood, in opposite ways.
b: Paul told the elders at Ephesus to shepherd "the church of God, which he acquired through his own blood" (Acts 20:28). Two things in that verse are debated. The Greek copies differ between "the church of God" and "the church of the Lord" (later ones read "of the Lord and God"), and the words for "his own blood" can also mean "the blood of his own one," that is, his Son (see the variant and the note at Acts 20:28). The point does not rest on that verse alone: Christ "offered himself" to God (Hebrews 9:14), lays down his life "by my own choice" (John 10:18), and "we were still sinners when Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). My reading: Atrahasis and the New Testament both tie human life to the blood of one who is divine, and the contrast is sharp. Here a lesser god is killed by other gods, unwilling, so they can rest, and his blood makes workers for their load. In the New Testament the Son gives himself freely, for those who wronged him, to make them free children of God (Galatians 4:4-7). I do not suggest that the New Testament draws on this poem. The likeness is one of the old questions humans ask, answered in two ways.

p: The gods spit on the clay. Jesus once spat, made clay, and opened a blind man's eyes.
b: Millard asked whether the gods' spitting was the life-giving act, or only a step in working the clay, and warned that it is "very different" from God's breathing into Adam (Genesis 2:7). John tells how Jesus "spat on the ground and made a paste of clay out of the spit, and smeared the clay on the man's eyes" (John 9:6). Irenaeus (about AD 180) read that act as Jesus showing "the hand of God" that first shaped Adam from the earth (Against Heresies 5.15.2). Differs: in the Gospel the one who makes clay is the Creator himself, healing what was made.

a: Second tablet of When the Gods Were Man
p: The late Sippar copy ends its tablet here and calls it the second tablet.
b: In the main Old Babylonian copy, the first tablet runs to line 416. But the late Sippar copy, a Neo-Babylonian tablet published by George and al-Rawi, ends here with a colophon calling it "the second tablet" of the poem, written "like its old copy." So later scribes cut the poem into more, shorter tablets. The note also shows they still knew the poem by its first line.

a: You butchered a god, along with his understanding
p: Mami reminds the gods what the work cost: a god, and his understanding with him.
b: The phrase qadu ṭēmišu makes the point that the god's understanding went into the clay with his flesh. Humans can plan and reason because they carry it. Read with 3:40, the poem seems to say that human reason is a borrowed god's mind, given so that humans can do the gods' work well.

a: You have given noise to humankind
p: Šaḫādu is a rare verb, "to give, present." Mami tells the gods they have given noise to humans.
b: SEAL glosses the verb šaḫādu "to give, present"; the SEAL editors note that it appears only here and once more in the poem (in Tablet II), and reject an older reading, "you have thrown off." The line says only that the gods have given rigmu, "noise," to humankind; it does not say whose noise it was. The noise will grow until Enlil cannot sleep and sends plague, drought and the Flood. On a possible link with the gods' own noise at 2:41, see the theory there.
orig: ta-aš-ta-aḫ-da ri-ig-ma a-na a-wi-lu-ti (taštaḫdā rigma ana awīlūti)

a: I have set up a release
p: The goddess proclaims a "release" for the gods. The same root names Israel's Jubilee "release."
b: Andurāru was the Babylonian word for a royal release: debts cancelled and debt-slaves set free. Jonathan Kaplan notes that the Hebrew deror of Leviticus 25:10, "proclaim release in the land," shares its root with Akkadian andurārum, and that King Ammi-saduqa, in whose reign the main copy of this poem was written (see the colophon of the first tablet), issued what Kaplan calls perhaps the most extensive such edict known. Differs: Mami's release frees gods by binding humans. The Bible's release frees people: Jesus read, "He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives" (Luke 4:18).

p: The gods give Mami a new name for her work: Mistress of All the Gods.
b: Freed from their load, the gods rename Mami bēlet kala ilī, "Mistress of all the gods." It explains her usual name Belet-ili, "Lady of the gods." Millard noted that the rejoicing gods gave her the title once the task was complete. A name given for a great deed is common in the Bible too (Genesis 32:28), though in Genesis 32:28 it is God who gives Jacob his new name.

p: Probably the room where a child is born and its fate is set.
b: Bīt šīmti, "the house of destiny," is restored from an Assyrian copy. The SEAL editors report William Moran's view, following Thorkild Jacobsen, that it is the chamber in which a child is born. In Babylonian belief a person's fate was fixed at birth by the gods.

p: Ninshiku is a title of Enki, the same title spelled naššiku and niššīku at 1:16.
b: The Assyrian copy reads Ninšiku Ea, and an Old Babylonian copy has traces of the same. It is a third spelling of the title written naššiku and niššīku at 1:16, which SEAL's glossary explains as "a title of Ea, prince"; SEAL's English here has "the prince Ea." The Plain keeps the line's form of the title and says "Enki" for Ea.

a: She recited the spell over and over
p: Mami repeats a spell while the birth goddesses tread the clay. Babylonian midwives also used birth spells.
b: Šiptu is an incantation. The verb form means she cast it again and again. The scene matches real Babylonian practice: SEAL lists many Old and Middle Babylonian incantations for birth. The poem presents the making of humans as the first birth, with all the rites that later births would follow. On the brick, see 3:99.

p: Mami nips fourteen lumps from the clay. Job uses a word of the same sound and sense for himself.
b: The Akkadian is kirṣī 14 uktarriṣ: she pinched off fourteen pieces, from karāṣu, "to pinch off." In Job, Elihu says, "I too was nipped off from clay" (Job 33:6), where the Hebrew verb is qorats, close in sound and meaning. The picture of a person as a lump pinched from the potter's clay was shared across the region. Fourteen is seven and seven: seven males and seven females (3:103-3:104).

p: A brick used at childbirth. Exodus also mentions birth stones.
b: The SEAL editors point to Marten Stol's study of birth in Babylonia (2000) for "the brick of birth," a brick used at childbirth. Exodus 1:16 mentions the ovnayim, "the two stones" of the birthstool, where the Hebrew midwives watched for the child. Here Mami sets the brick between the two rows of clay, as a midwife prepares a birth.

p: A knife "of the reed bed" that cuts the navel cord: the midwife's blade.
b: The old copy keeps only "... the navel cord ...". The Assyrian copy gives the whole line: she drew the luṭû of the appāru, "the one that cuts the navel cord." SEAL glosses luṭû as a kind of dagger and appāru as "reed-bed, marsh"; the SEAL editors explain the verb as "unsheathe," as of a weapon. The phrase says where the knife belongs, not what it is made of. The detail shows again that the poem tells the first birth as a model for every birth.

t: Seven and seven, male and female
p: Mami's helpers shape seven males and seven females. Genesis tells of one man and one woman.
b: The poem makes humans as a group: seven males and seven females, shaped by fourteen birth goddesses. Genesis tells of one pair: "male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27), and of one man and one woman joined as "one flesh" (Genesis 2:24). Jesus and Paul build on that single pair (Matthew 19:4-6; Acts 17:26). Agrees that humans are made male and female from the start; differs on how many and on who makes them.

p: The verb probably means "veil" or "crown," as at a wedding, though its sense here is debated.
b: SEAL glosses the verb kullulu "to veil, crown." The SEAL editors understand the birth goddess as veiling the newly made figures and pairing them two by two. My reading: veiling and pairing may look ahead to the marriages that the following lines of the tablet describe (chapter 4).

a: The scribe's count of lines for this column: 58.
t: A line count on the edge
p: The old copy has a bare number, 58, on the lower edge: the scribe counted the lines of the column.
b: On the lower edge of the old copy, below the last line of its second column, the scribe wrote "58." The SEAL editors call it "a scribal remark counting the lines so far"; the column holds 58 lines, lines 57 to 114 of the poem. Scribes counted lines to check that a copy was complete, and the same scribe gives the whole tablet's count in the colophon. The number is not part of the story.

a: He spoke to his brother Anu.
p: Two later copies have this pair of lines twice; the old copy has it once (2:146-2:147).
b: These two lines (2:144-2:145, lines 167a-b) are found only in the late Sippar copy bb and the Assyrian copy K(+)M. In both, they say almost exactly what the next two lines say: Enlil ("the god") was afraid, and he spoke to his brother Anu; in those two copies 2:145 and 2:147 are the same words, izzakkar ana aḫišu Anu. The old copy has only the second pair, and calls Anu "the warrior" (2:147). So the repetition is in the copies, not a slip of the Plain; the later scribes seem to have kept two forms of one couplet side by side.

a: The scribe's count of lines for this column: 55 ...
p: At the foot of its fourth column the old copy has a count, 55, with a damaged sign after it.
b: The old copy ends its fourth column, just before 3:56, with a bare number: 55 and a damaged sign. The SEAL editors read "55[+2?]," that is, possibly 57, and the question mark shows they are not sure. Like the 58 at 2:85, it is the scribe's count of the column's lines, not part of the story.
